e.t: This word means “free” or “free of charge,” describing something provided without requiring payment. It functions as an adjective, identifying what is offered without cost rather than something purchased or owed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 9:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: something is given or done without charge. The word therefore emphasizes the absence of financial cost.

Amethyst is the name of a stone. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, and its English rendering is consistently “amethyst.” It appears in Revelation 21:20, but the verse text is not included here, so the word’s broader significance in that passage cannot be described from this lexical entry alone. Its basic meaning is simply the stone’s name.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to go away”: it describes someone leaving a place or moving away from people or circumstances. Its focus is the action of departure, rather than the reason for leaving or what happens afterward. The word appears 117 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is a common way of expressing movement away. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word refers to a chief priest, especially a high-ranking priest who held authority among the priests. It identifies a leading priest rather than an ordinary priest. In the Greek New Testament, the word appears 122 times, showing its repeated use for prominent priestly figures in the Gospel accounts, Acts, and Hebrews. The wording can be rendered “chief priest” or “high-priest,” with the surrounding passage clarifying the particular person or group being identified.

Balaam is a personal name—the name of a person mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a proper name used to identify him. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament: once in 2 Peter, once in Jude, and once in Revelation. Understanding what Balaam represents in any particular passage requires reading that passage and its surrounding context.

This word means “book” or “books,” referring to a written work or collection of written material. It is a noun used for documents within the Greek New Testament, including written records associated with genealogy, Scripture, lists, and other recorded matters. The word occurs 10 times in 10 New Testament verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its basic meaning remains focused on a book as a written record; the surrounding passage determines which particular book or collection is meant in each occurrence.

This word refers to demons—spiritual beings presented in the New Testament as active against people and opposed to God’s work. It is a plural noun, though the same word may be rendered “demon” when referring to one. The word appears 63 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that references to demons occur across the Gospels and in other New Testament writings. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the action or teaching connected with it.

As a verb, it can express an opening that has taken place or is taking place, with the surrounding sentence showing who or what is involved. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, including uses rendered “opened” in Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its basic meaning remains the same whether the object is physical or understood from the sentence.

This word means “teaching”—the communication of instruction or what is taught. It can describe teaching as an activity or the instruction being given, whether that teaching is faithful or misleading; the surrounding passage determines its particular force. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 21 times, including passages that speak of human traditions, spiritual instruction, and teaching that helps believers grow. Its central idea remains the transmission of instruction to others.

This word means “deceitful”: it describes someone or something that uses deception rather than acting openly and honestly. It points to a lack of straightforwardness and to conduct intended to mislead. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:13. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the character or practice of deception.

This word refers to a slave or servant—someone serving under another person’s authority. Its central meaning is a person whose service and obligations are defined by a master. It can also describe a female servant or female slave, and the related idea of being enslaved appears among its listed meanings. The word occurs 129 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact force depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains devoted or obligated service under authority.

e.t: This word means “to uproot”: to pull a plant out of the ground, removing it from its place by the roots. It is a verb describing decisive removal rather than merely cutting or damaging something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including passages where plants or tree-like images are described as being uprooted. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains removal from the ground or established position.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to make straight” or “to straighten.” It describes an action that removes crookedness and brings something into a direct, orderly course. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming an object or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, showing a focused but repeated use of this straightforward idea. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word describes something “admirable” or “commendable”—something rightly regarded with respect and approval. It points to a quality that deserves a favorable judgment, rather than merely something pleasant or attractive. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Philippians 4:8. Since the verse text is not included here, its precise application in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic sense. The word directs attention to what merits thoughtful approval and praise.

This word means hostility: an attitude or condition of opposition and enmity between people or sides. It describes active division rather than simple difference or disagreement. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, including passages that speak of hostility between people, hostility toward God, and hostility associated with friendship with the world. It can therefore describe both an inward disposition and an outward barrier that separates. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to care for.” It expresses active concern and attentive care toward someone, describing a person who looks after another rather than treating that person with indifference. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains personal, caring attention.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to reap” or “reaping”—gathering a crop after it has grown. It is a verb describing the act of harvesting, and it can also describe someone who regularly reaps. The word appears 21 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of birds not sowing or reaping and servants being held accountable for what they do. Its central picture remains the same: receiving or gathering the result of what has been cultivated. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to ordinary farming or a figurative harvest.

This word describes something as belonging to a particular person or group—“one’s own,” “one’s own/private,” or “private.” It points to what is personal, individually possessed, or set apart from what is shared publicly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 114 times, showing that this idea is used broadly in different kinds of statements. Its precise force in any passage depends on what person, group, or possession the surrounding sentence identifies.

e.t: This word means “Israelite” and refers to a person belonging to Israel. Its plural sense is “Israelites,” naming the people identified with Israel. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, functioning as a designation for people rather than describing an action, quality, or event. It appears across John, Acts, Romans, and 2 Corinthians, so its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it occurs; the surrounding verse supplies the specific point being made about the Israelite or Israelites mentioned.

This word means “Caesar,” referring to the Roman emperor or imperial authority. It is used in the New Testament for the ruler whose government stood over Judea and the wider Roman world. The word appears 29 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages where people speak about giving Caesar what belongs to him and where believers connected with Caesar’s household are mentioned. As a name or title, it identifies the imperial ruler rather than describing a general quality or action.

This word describes people who despise what they hear and respond with scorn—a “despiser” or “scoffer.” It refers to a person marked by contempt rather than humble attention, so its basic sense is someone who treats a message or warning as unworthy of respect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:41. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to contemptuous rejection.

This word means “breaking,” referring plainly to the act or process of breaking something. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Luke 24:35 and once in Acts 2:42. The same basic meaning is represented in both occurrences. The surrounding verse and passage determine exactly what is being broken or how the action functions there, but the word itself centers on breaking rather than on a broader spiritual or doctrinal idea.

The word means “mina,” the name of a monetary unit. It refers to a measured sum of money rather than to a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, all in six verses of Luke 19, where the repeated term identifies the same kind of monetary amount. Its plural rendering, “minas,” refers to more than one mina. The word’s precise significance in each sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the named unit of money.

e.t: This word means “now” or “present”. It points to the current time, whether referring to what is happening at this moment or to a present situation. It can distinguish the present from what happened earlier or what will happen later. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 147 times, showing that it is a common time-word used across many kinds of sentences. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the time that is currently at hand.

This word means “manager,” referring to someone entrusted with overseeing another person’s household, property, or responsibilities. It describes a role of delegated authority: the manager does not own what is placed in his care but is responsible for handling it faithfully. The word appears ten times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that use it for household administration and for people entrusted with responsibilities in service to God. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to talk,” referring to speaking with others in ordinary conversation. It describes verbal interaction rather than naming a particular message, topic, or outcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses in Luke and Acts. Its basic sense remains simple: people are speaking together. The surrounding passage determines who is talking and what they are discussing, but the word itself emphasizes the act of conversation. It can therefore be understood naturally wherever the text describes people talking with one another.

This word means “transgression”: an act of violating or stepping beyond an expressed command or boundary. It describes wrongdoing as a breach of what has been required, rather than merely a general weakness or mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing especially in Romans and Hebrews. Its uses include references to transgression in relation to law, commandments, and accountable human action. The surrounding verse determines the specific command or boundary involved, but the central idea remains a transgression against an established requirement.

e.t: This word means “to boast”: to speak proudly about oneself or one’s achievements. It functions as a verb, describing an act of proud self-expression rather than simply possessing a good quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 13:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, which are needed to show exactly how this boasting is being described.

This word means “width,” referring to how broad or wide something is. It is a noun used for a measurable dimension, alongside other dimensions when describing size or extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times in three verses, including Ephesians 3:18 and Revelation 21:16. Its meaning remains straightforward: it identifies the side-to-side breadth of something, whether described as part of a physical measurement or used among a set of dimensions. The surrounding verse determines what is being measured.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to add” or “to confer,” describing the act of contributing something or presenting it for consideration. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Galatians. Its basic sense concerns adding information, counsel, or agreement to what is already being considered. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis falls on contributing something or conferring with others.

This word means “acceptance”: receiving someone or something favorably rather than rejecting it. It is a noun that describes the act or result of being received with approval or welcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 11:15. Its basic sense is broad enough to describe favorable reception, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being accepted and what significance that acceptance has there.

This word refers to a Stoic, a person associated with the Stoic philosophical school. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 17:18. The word identifies a person by philosophical affiliation rather than describing a general emotion, behavior, or spiritual quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a Stoic—someone connected with Stoic thought. This is a Greek New Testament word and should be understood within that corpus.

It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Ephesians 2:5 and Colossians 2:13. Its precise force in either verse is understood more fully from the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “to dine with” or “to eat with” someone. It describes sharing a meal in company with others, rather than merely eating alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, in passages involving people gathered around meals or dining places. The word therefore focuses on participation in a shared meal and the people present together. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense is eating together with others.

This word means “chosen together with” or “chosen with,” describing someone selected alongside another person or group. It expresses shared choosing rather than selection in isolation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, at 1 Peter 5:13, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains association through being chosen together with someone else, not merely being present with them. This is a lexical description, while the verse context determines whom it identifies and why that designation matters.

This word refers to a carpenter or craftsman—someone who works skillfully with materials to make or build things. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3. Both passages use it as an ordinary occupational description, identifying a person by his trade rather than expressing a spiritual title or special role. The word can therefore be understood broadly as a skilled maker or builder, while “carpenter” is the consistent English rendering in these occurrences.

This word means “named” or “by name,” referring to identifying someone through a personal name. It functions as a naming expression rather than describing a person’s character, actions, or status. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 27:57. The normal idea is simple: a person is identified by the name given or known to others. The surrounding verse determines how that naming expression functions in its particular sentence.

It is an adverb, so it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 16:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is conduct marked by practical wisdom or clever judgment.

This word describes something that dawns, shines through, or is transparent. It can refer to the arrival of light, as when darkness gives way to brightness, or to a clear, see-through quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Peter and once in Revelation. Its two uses show that the word can describe either light breaking through or something marked by clarity and transparency, with the surrounding sentence determining which aspect is intended.
